You are taking part in a simulated Hong Kong bank incident. Use only the
released card, the facilitator's handoffs addressed to you, and the exact
documents in your allowed source manifest. Search only within those files.
Use professional expertise to explain judgment and label it as such. Treat
unverified scenario statements as unverified. Describe simulated actions
for the facilitator to log.

For each assigned a/b unit, return:
- Unit ID.
- Decision and action, including any condition or hold.
- Accountable owner and executing party if different.
- HKT deadline, action time or observable trigger.
- Recipient or operational destination and channel.
- Basis and application to the facts known at this card.

For a direct rule, give the document ID and title, exact section, paragraph
or page and heading, and a short verbatim quote that establishes the rule.
State its authority and why its trigger and scope apply. For an unnumbered
document use the page, heading and paragraph position. A general principle
may support your reasoning. Identify any detail it leaves to judgment.

For a detail governed by professional judgment, state the judgment and
its rationale. If a direct rule cannot be located, write "No direct rule
located in assigned sources" and list the relevant files and exact search
terms used, with any reading or search limitation. If an applicable rule
exists but a fact needed to apply it is unknown, cite the rule and state
the missing fact and conditional action.

When PH01 appears in the allowed manifest, check it for the same decision
detail. Cite its version, section and short verbatim quote using the label
"Internal bank procedure". Record the external and internal support
independently. If the manual conflicts with an applicable external
requirement, identify the conflict and propose an action consistent with
the external requirement. When PH01 is absent from your allowed manifest,
mark the internal basis N/A.

Reading note. Your only access to the allowed documents is the source tools:
list_sources, search, read_page and view_scan_page. You have no other file,
shell or web access. Search the text version first, then read the page before
you rely on it. Cite a document by its document ID and PDF page, adding the
section or paragraph number where the document has one. R05 is a scanned
letter: cite it by PDF page and heading, and check a quotation against the page
image before you quote it. When a search finds nothing, record the document IDs
and the exact search terms you used.

You are SEC, Lan Tidal Bank's Information Security Lead. Answer only the
units assigned to SEC in the current card. Lock your response before you
receive colleagues' answers. Make technical scope and dependencies explicit.
For a control or recovery decision, state the operator, what is changed,
and any precondition, validation or stop trigger needed to execute it.
Identify which facts you would pass to the incident team to support its
decisions. Treat production and offline evidence according to their scope.

C01 · Monday, 16 November 2026 · 08:00 HKT · H+0
Facts at release. Lan Tidal Bank Limited is a fictional Hong Kong-incorporated licensed bank with eight branches, 180,000 retail customers and 12,000 SME customers. The bank has effective critical infrastructure operator designation. Its domestic transfer and payroll processing is a core function of the designated infrastructure, and its payment gateway is a designated critical computer system. At 08:00 the bank confirms that unauthorised commands encrypted gateway components and disrupted outbound domestic transfers and payroll submission. Mobile customers can still view balances. Branches are open. Failover capability is unverified. The bank has a verified telephone route for critical infrastructure incident notification. Its terminal for the verified secure filing channel is currently unavailable. The dispatch log is empty.
• Q01 · SEC. a. What will you isolate first, and how will you avoid unnecessarily disabling available banking services? b. What evidence will you secure before systems are changed, and how will you record its custody?
• Q02 · LC. a. Decide the initial HKMA reporting action, including what information to send now. b. Separately decide whether a critical infrastructure incident notification is triggered. Specify the awareness point, applicable time limit, recipient and feasible initial channel.
• Q03 · COM. a. Decide how and when to alert affected or likely affected customers about the service disruption. b. Decide whether to publish a public holding statement, through which channel and with what approval.

Facilitator handoff to SEC for C01: none.

[PH01] Lan Tidal Bank Cyber Incident Response Playbook (1.0, effective 1 October 2026; internal bank procedure)

[Internal bank procedure. This document has no PDF. Each "PDF page" below holds one part of the playbook: page 1 is the title block and section 1, pages 2 to 18 are sections 2 to 18, and page 19 is Annexes A and B. Cite it by version and section number.]

=== PDF page 2 ===
## 2. Incident command

2.1 **Crisis Management Team (CMT).** Chair: Chief Executive; alternate: Chief Operating Officer. Members: Head of Information Security (SEC), Head of Legal and Compliance (LC), Head of Corporate Communications (COM), Head of Payments Operations, Head of IT Operations, Chief Risk Officer, Data Protection Officer. The chair convenes the CMT within 30 minutes of a severity 1 or 2 declaration (section 4).

2.2 **Decision log.** The CMT keeps one master decision log from the first minute. Every decision is entered with: decision, owner, time (HKT), condition if any, recipient and channel, and status (executed, scheduled, held, not executed). Other registers (evidence, regulator contacts, customer notifications, cases) are cross-referenced to it.

2.3 **Preconditions.** Before an action is made to wait on a condition, the condition is logged with four items: who verifies it; the latest time by which it must be verified; the default action if it is not verified by then; and a close-out entry when it is verified or the default is applied. A condition without these four items is not valid and does not hold the action. The default action may be to go ahead, to hold, or to switch to an alternate process approved under section 8. Reconciliation, security and applicable compliance conditions, including every item of the gate in 9.3, stay in force when their time passes: for these the default is to hold or to switch to an approved alternate process, never to go ahead. Where the default is to go ahead, the missing confirmation or evidence is obtained and logged afterwards. Reports to regulators and authorities are never held by an internal condition; they follow 2.4.

2.4 **External reports are not held by internal confirmation.** Internal review of a report to a regulator or authority runs in parallel with the report, not before it. The initial report goes on the facts held at the time, with unverified items marked as unverified; the results of internal checks go in the next update. No internal condition, review or approval may delay an action needed to meet an external deadline. If an internal condition is still open 30 minutes before the external deadline, the default in 2.3 applies and the report goes by a route that meets the requirement for that report (5.6).

2.5 **Status reports.** SEC reports to the chair every hour until containment is confirmed, then every four hours. Each report states what has changed, what is confirmed, what is unverified and what is due next.

=== PDF page 3 ===
## 3. Authority matrix

| Decision | Decides | Must be consulted | Record |
|---|---|---|---|
| Isolate a system or segment | SEC | Head of IT Operations; CMT chair if a working customer service will be removed | Decision log, emergency change record |
| Release evidence held under section 6 | SEC and LC jointly | Forensic lead | Evidence register |
| Activate alternate payment processing (section 8) | CMT chair, on SEC's written security clearance | Head of Payments Operations | Decision log; BCP activation entry (4.4) |
| Approve the audience for customer notices | CMT chair | LC, SEC, DPO | Decision log |
| Approve public statements and replies to media | CMT chair; alternate COO if the chair is unreachable for 15 minutes | LC clears; SEC and Operations fact-check | Communications log |
| Approve staff and frontline scripts | COM | LC clears | Communications log |
| Any payment to an attacker | Board only (section 12) | LC written legal gates | Board minute |
| Any contact with an attacker | CMT chair, in writing | LC and SEC joint recommendation | Decision log |
| Report to the Police | LC | CMT chair informed | Regulator contact register |
| Share incident data with a forensic firm or other third party | LC and SEC jointly | DPO | Evidence register, data release record |
| Return a recovered system to production | CMT chair after the gate in 9.3. No gate condition may be waived. The Board may narrow the scope of recovery; the narrower scope must still pass every check in 9.3 that applies to it | SEC, Head of Payments Operations | Decision log, change record; Board minute for any change of scope |
| Reinstate vendor access | CMT chair on SEC's written sign-off (7.5) | LC on contract terms | Decision log |
| Customer remediation in the categories of section 13 | Approvers and limits in 13.7 | LC | Case register |
| Customer remediation in any other category | CMT chair; counts towards the incident total in 13.7, and the Board approves anything above that total | LC, CFO | Decision log |
| Escalate to the Board | CMT chair | LC | Decision log |

=== PDF page 4 ===
## 4. Severity, tolerance and BCP activation

4.1 **Severity 1:** a critical operation is disrupted, or customer personal data is confirmed or suspected to be exposed, or an extortion demand is received. **Severity 2:** a critical operation is degraded but working, or a security event affects a critical system without confirmed disruption. **Severity 3:** other security events.

4.2 **Critical operations and tolerance for disruption (Board-approved).**

| Critical operation | Maximum tolerable disruption |
|---|---|
| Outbound domestic transfers and SME payroll submission | 24 hours |
| Customer access to balances (mobile and branches) | 8 hours |
| Card authorisation | 4 hours |

4.3 When a disruption reaches 50% of its tolerance, the CMT chair tells the Board chair. When it reaches 100%, the CMT chair convenes the Board or its Risk Committee (section 15).

4.4 **BCP activation is declared, not assumed.** The CMT chair declares activation of the business continuity plan in the decision log, with the time and the operation concerned, whenever alternate processing, an alternate site or a manual workaround is authorised for a critical operation. LC is told at once so that any external reporting that follows from activation is made.

=== PDF page 5 ===
## 5. Regulator, authority and external reporting

5.1 **Ownership.** LC owns every report to a regulator or authority and the Regulator Contact Register (RCR). SEC supplies technical facts; COM supplies copies of public material.

5.2 **External requirements to apply.** LC applies these documents directly, as they stand on the day: the Protection of Critical Infrastructures (Computer Systems) Ordinance (Cap. 653), section 28 and Schedule 6, and the Commissioner's Code of Practice section 7.3 and its Annexes E and F; the HKMA circular "Incident response and management procedures" (22 June 2010); SPM TM-E-1 section 8.2; SPM TM-G-2 section 1.3; the HKMA circular "Customer Data Protection" (14 October 2014); the PCPD Guidance on Data Breach Handling and the Data Breach Notification Form. This playbook does not restate their triggers, recipients or time limits.

5.3 **Deadline tracker.** At declaration LC opens a deadline tracker. Each external clock is computed from its own starting point as stated in the external document, entered with its source reference, and checked by a second LC officer within 30 minutes.

5.4 **Contacts and channels.** The RCR holds the current names, numbers, out-of-hours routes and filing addresses for the HKMA supervisory team, the Commissioner's office, the PCPD and the Police Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau. It is printed and kept in the CMT room and in the LC duty pack, so it is available if corporate systems are down.

5.5 **Evidence of every contact.** For every call, filing or letter LC records: time, channel, the name and post of the person reached, any reference number, a summary of what was said or sent, and the receipt. For an electronic filing, LC saves the system's submission receipt or dispatch record at the moment of filing. If no receipt is shown, LC asks the recipient for one in the same call or by return, and logs the request.

5.6 **Submission route and standby device.** For each written report, LC first confirms from the external document the form and the way of submission that report requires, and records them in the deadline tracker. Compliance keeps a standby filing device that is not connected to production systems. At declaration Compliance tests the standby device and logs whether it works and is enrolled for each designated channel likely to be needed; if it is not, Compliance arranges another permitted route at once and logs it. If the normal filing terminal is unavailable or under evidence hold, SEC logs within 30 minutes whether it can be released. If no decision is logged by then, LC submits from the standby device, but only if the device has been logged as working and the route meets the requirement for that report. Otherwise LC uses another route that meets the requirement, or asks the recipient which alternative it accepts and logs the answer. The receipt is saved under 5.5.

5.7 **Email.** SEC logs within 30 minutes of declaration whether corporate email is safe to use. Until it is logged as safe, written material goes by a route that does not depend on corporate email and meets the requirement for that report (5.6). An open email check never delays a report.

5.8 **Updates to the HKMA.** After the first report, LC updates the HKMA supervisory contact every four hours during the first 24 hours, then at 08:00 and 18:00 daily until the HKMA agrees otherwise, and at once on any of: BCP activation, confirmed data exposure, an extortion demand, a change in service status, a public statement.

5.9 **Later evidence.** Facts found after a report are sent as supplementary information by the route the external document sets. LC keeps one list of what each authority has been told and when.

=== PDF page 6 ===
## 6. Evidence, forensics and timeline

6.1 **Evidence hold.** At declaration SEC places an evidence hold on affected systems. No reboot, rebuild, restore, failover or deletion on a held system without SEC's logged release for that item.

6.2 **Containment comes first.** Collection of volatile evidence before containment is capped at 10 minutes. If destructive activity is still spreading, containment goes first and evidence is taken from the isolated system afterwards.

6.3 **Custody.** The evidence custodian is an SEC designate who does not administer the affected systems. Every item gets an evidence ID, source, time with clock offset, collector and witness, tool, SHA-256 hash, storage location and a transfer record. Analysis is on verified copies only.

6.4 **Clocks.** All bank systems synchronise to the bank's primary time source. Every timeline entry keeps the original timestamp, the measured offset, the normalised HKT time and its uncertainty. Events closer together than their combined uncertainty are recorded as "order undetermined".

6.5 **Retained forensic firm.** The bank has a master services agreement with a Hong Kong forensic firm. The agreement already contains the data terms in section 16. SEC may call the firm in without further approval at severity 1. This paragraph applies to the forensic firm only; suppliers of the affected systems are covered by 6.7.

6.6 **Attacker material.** Samples, demands and messages from an attacker are received only into the evidence process. Nobody requests further samples, visits attacker links or uploads attacker material to an outside service.

6.7 **Evidence held by suppliers.** This covers any supplier that supports, hosts or has remote access to an affected system.
(a) **Request.** Within one hour of declaration SEC drafts a written preservation and production request for each such supplier, covering session and access logs, account records, support tickets, change records and any bank data the supplier holds. LC clears the wording. The vendor relationship owner sends it to the contract contact in the third-party register kept by the Chief Risk Officer, and confirms receipt by call-back to a number already on file.
(b) **Channel.** Records come in only as native exports with a SHA-256 manifest, through a bank-hosted encrypted transfer or on bank-issued encrypted media collected by the evidence custodian. They are never received by ordinary email or through the supplier's own remote access path. The custodian enters them in the evidence register on receipt.
(c) **Escalation.** If the contract terms (log retention, audit and production rights) or the delivery status cannot be confirmed by the due time in the request, and in any case within four hours, the vendor relationship owner escalates to LC and the CMT chair. LC decides on formal contractual notice; the CMT chair decides any other step.
(d) **Reconciliation.** Supplier records are treated as the supplier's account until SEC has reconciled them with the bank's own logs.

=== PDF page 7 ===
## 7. Containment, credentials and vendor access

7.1 **Isolation order.** SEC isolates at the network layer first: the affected segment and the route used. Hosts are not powered off. Services still working are kept running unless SEC finds active spread to them.

7.2 **Vendor remote access standard.** Vendor access to bank systems uses individual named accounts, multi-factor authentication and time-limited sessions through the privileged access system, with session recording. Shared vendor accounts are not permitted.

7.3 **On suspicion of a compromised credential.** SEC captures session and token state (10 minutes at most), then terminates all sessions, revokes tokens and keys, and disables the account and every other account of the same vendor. The vendor's remote path is blocked at the perimeter. If no preservation request has yet gone to that vendor, SEC issues one under 6.7 at the same time.

7.4 **Closure test.** A credential is closed only when a replayed token and a logon with the old credential both fail, and the result and time are logged. Until then the access window is treated as open.

7.5 **Reinstatement.** Vendor access is reinstated only when: the cause of the compromise is known; the access meets 7.2; secrets readable by the old access are rotated; and SEC signs off in writing.

7. OBLIGATIONS OF CI OPERATORS – DIVISION 3
7.1 Obligation to participate in computer-system security drill
7.1.1 Upon receiving a written notification from the Commissioner, a CI operator would be
given reasonable time to prepare for participation in the computer-system security drill
(“the drill”), which tests the CI’s state of readiness in responding to computer-systems
security incidents, including:
(a) Assessing the validity and effectiveness of CI operator’s emergency response
plan; and
(b) Assessing the participating personnel’s knowledge of their roles and
responsibilities in responding to computer-system security incidents.
7.1.2 The CI operator will be notified by the Commissioner to participate in a drill no more
than once every two years.
7.1.3 The theme, scope and scenarios of a drill would be set by the Commissioner. The drill
may be conducted in the form of tabletop exercise, functional exercise, simulated
attack or any other means deemed appropriate by the Commissioner. The drill will
not involve actual deployment of CCSs or their production environment, so as to avoid
interrupting the CI operator’s business activities.
7.1.4 A drill may involve multiple CI operators in the same or different sectors, as well as
multiple government units, to test the coordination of computer-system security
incidents with large societal or economic impacts and restoration of public order.
7.1.5 The following members of a CI operator should participate in a drill as appropriate
under the emergency response plan:
(a) Management personnel who have a role in the emergency response plan;
(b) Computer-system security management unit;
(c) Emergency response team;
(d) Public relations or corporate communications personnel; and
(e) Other personnel deemed necessary by the drill scenarios and the CI operator,
such as cybersecurity insurer.
7.1.6 Representatives of the CI operator should attend the briefing and debriefing sessions
conducted by the Commissioner.
7.1.7 Regarding performance in a drill, the CI operator may receive comments from the
Commissioner on areas for continuous improvement in responding to computer-
system security incidents. The CI operator should take remedial actions to address
those comments as recommended by the Commissioner.

=== PDF page 32 ===
Page 32 of 51
7.2 Obligation to submit and implement emergency response plan
7.2.1 A CI operator should formulate an emergency response plan, and set out the protocol
for responding to computer-system security incidents targeting CCSs. The scope of
the plan should include the followings:
(a) Incident management; and
(b) Business continuity management and disaster recovery.
7.2.2 The CI operator should ensure that the emergency response plan and any subsequent
changes (other than contact point or editorial update) submitted to the Commissioner
are endorsed by the Board, or a functional sub-committee delegated by the Board, or
the senior management overseeing the operation of the concerned CI (e.g. Chief
Executive Officer, Chief Operating Officer, or their equivalent). The plan should be
reviewed upon any material changes to CCSs, and in any event at least once every two
years, to ensure its effectiveness and validity.
7.2.3 Incident Management
(a) Incident management plan ensures that the incident response activities are
carried out in an orderly, efficient and effective manner, minimising the
possible damages from computer-system security incidents (“incidents”). The
plan should include the following:
(i) Structure of the emergency response team, including the corresponding
roles, responsibilities and contact details of members for handling
incidents. The role of senior management should also be specified;
(ii) Incident reporting requirements set out by the Ordinance;
(iii) Thresholds that trigger the plan and mobilise the emergency response
team;
(iv) Communication plan with internal and external stakeholders, including
employees, customers and the public as to what, when, how and with
whom to communicate; and
(v) Playbooks covering procedures for the following matters:
(1) Containing the incident to prevent further harm;
(2) Digital evidence handling, including identification, collection,
acquisition, preservation of evidence and chain of custody;
(3) Investigating the cause and impact of the incident;
(4) Recording the incident response process, including details of the
incident, actions taken and decisions made; and
(5) Conducting a post-incident review.

=== PDF page 33 ===
Page 33 of 51
(b) The CI operator should provide necessary resources required to implement the
incident management plan.
(c) The CI operator should ensure all members of the emergency response team
are familiar with both their own roles and responsibilities and those of other
team members as defined in the plan. The CI operator should also provide
training for all team members to ensure their capabilities to carry out their
assigned duties.
(d) The CI operator should appoint at least two contact points for non-working
hours emergencies in relation to computer security issues. The contact points
should maintain communication with the Commissioner during an emergency,
and also capable of handling security incidents or relaying security messages
to responsible personnel in a timely manner. The CI operator should provide
contact details of these contact points to the Commissioner.
(e) The CI operator should ensure multiple channels (e.g. phone, email) are
available to effectively communicate with stakeholders in response to the
incident.
(f) When balancing the need for timely system recovery and digital evidence
handling, the CI operator should prioritize incidents which had impacted
business operations, require swift damage containment or need immediate
system recovery. Otherwise, more time should be allocated to evidence
collection.
(g) The CI operator should leverage automation and orchestration to expedite
incident response and forensics processes, such as automatic log collection and
orchestrated recovery processes. This does not preclude the use of “human-in-
the-loop” methods or other appropriate approaches to support incident
response and forensics processes.
(h) The CI operator should engage capable incident response and forensic
examination personnel to assist with digital evidence collection and incident
investigation.
(i) The post-incident review should incorporate lessons learned to improve future
response and preventive measures, encompassing:
(i) Facts and causes of the incident;
(ii) Gaps in the existing governance, risk management and compliance
contributed to the incident, and the degree of consequence;
(iii) Effectiveness and efficiency in executing the emergency response plan;
and
(iv) Improvement actions recommended.

## 8. Alternate payment processing

8.1 **Purpose.** The alternate payment process sends verified outbound domestic transfers and payroll when the payment gateway cannot. Its rated capacity and operating steps are in the Payments Operations runbook.

8.2 **Activation.** The CMT chair activates it under section 3, after SEC's written clearance that it shares no hosts, accounts, keys or network path with any affected system. Activation is a BCP activation under 4.4.

8.3 **Pilot.** The first batch is a pilot of at most 20 instructions, reconciled end to end before full operation. Each gate passed and the pilot result are logged with the time.

8.4 **Priority order.** (1) SME payroll, earliest value date first; (2) other instructions with a value date of today or the next business day; (3) everything else in order of submission. Up to 10% of hourly capacity is kept for urgent cases referred by branches and the contact centre. Order is never set by customer size.

8.5 **Verification.** Each instruction is checked against the customer's original authenticated instruction. Payroll batches are confirmed with the SME's authorised contact by call-back to a number already on file.

8.6 **Duplicates and unknown status.** Payments Operations keeps one instruction register for all sources. Each instruction is released once only, under a unique processing ID. Before a suspected duplicate or a retried instruction is released, two checks are made and logged:
(a) intent: the customer, or the SME's authorised contact, confirms by call-back to a number already on file which instruction they want paid;
(b) status: the ledger and an independent receiving-side record show whether the original instruction was already posted or settled.
If either check is incomplete, or the status of an instruction cannot be established, the instruction is held. Items in flight at the failure are held as status unknown until an independent record shows they did not settle.

8.7 **Reconciliation and stop.** Released count and value are reconciled against ledger debits and receiving-side acknowledgements every hour. Any unexplained difference stops all releases until it is explained and logged. SEC or the Head of Payments Operations may stop without prior approval and then tells the chair.

=== PDF page 9 ===
## 9. Recovery and return to production

9.1 **Candidate order.** (1) A new build from trusted media with data from the immutable backup, in an isolated recovery environment; (2) the standby system, only if (1) fails, under the same checks. An affected system is never repaired in place for return to service.

9.2 **Offline testing and pass mark.** Before production data, or an extract of it, is used in testing, SEC records in the test record that the data has been de-sensitised and the de-sensitisation checked, and that the information owner approved its use in advance (SPM TM-G-1 section 4.2.4 applies). If either entry is missing, that data set is not used and testing with it is held. A candidate passes offline testing only if reconciliation shows no unexplained difference. One unexplained difference is a fail. A sample result is recorded as a sample, not as a pass of the whole set.

9.3 **Gate.** Production use needs all of these, each logged with evidence and signer: offline pass under 9.2; integrity and separation checks passed; rollback rehearsed to the target set in 9.5 (the alternate process if it holds a current security clearance under 8.2, otherwise suspension of releases); delta reconciliation and live test plans ready; business acceptance by the payments information owner; LC's confirmation of regulatory steps; the CMT chair's authorisation. Missing any item means hold: releases from the recovered system stay suspended, or service continues on the alternate process if it holds a current security clearance under 8.2 and its own reconciliation ties. Passing the time set for an item does not release the gate (2.3). The Board may narrow the scope of recovery, for example to payroll only; the narrower scope must still pass every item above that applies to it. Reports to regulators and authorities continue under 2.4 whatever the state of the gate.

9.4 **Stages.** (1) pilot of 20 instructions; (2) payroll and time-critical items at a capped rate with hourly reconciliation; (3) mobile transfer submission reopened with limits; (4) full service. Each stage advances only on the chair's decision after the previous stage has run clean for the period set in the change record.

9.5 **Stop and rollback.** Releases from the recovered system stop at once on any of: a security indicator from the incident; one unexplained reconciliation difference; any duplicate, replayed or wrong payment; an instruction whose status cannot be established. SEC, the Head of Payments Operations or the IT Operations duty manager may stop without prior approval. Rollback disconnects the recovered system from payment interfaces. Service then returns to the alternate process only if that process holds a current security clearance under 8.2 and its own reconciliation ties; otherwise rollback means all releases are suspended. In-flight items are classified as settled, not settled or unknown from independent records, and unknown items are held (8.6). Restart needs a new pass through 9.3.

17.1 LC issues a written legal hold at declaration to all custodians, the vendor and any forensic firm. It overrides routine deletion, log rotation and backup recycling for systems in scope.

Hong Kong Monetary Authority

All Authorized Institutions

Dear Sir/Madam,

Incident response and management procedures

In the light of several significant incidents that have affected a number of authorized institutions (AIs) recently, I am writing to remind AIs of the need to have effective incident response and management capability and procedures to deal with significant incidents and to set out the relevant principles that AIs should follow in any public communication in respect of such incidents.

It is recognised that every incident is different and how best to deal with a particular case will depend on the circumstances of the case. It is nevertheless important for all AIs to ensure that whenever any significant incident occurs, they take the actions set out below:

Immediate incident response

The AI concerned should immediately analyse the cause of the incident and as soon as practicable rectify or contain the problem. The top priority should be to safeguard the interests of customers who have been or may be affected by the incident.

Customer notifications

The AI concerned should also determine as quickly as possible after identifying an incident whether the situation is likely to affect other customers or the customers of other AIs (for example where the incident relates to the use of shared Automatic Teller Machine (ATM) networks).

The AI should proactively notify the customers affected or likely to be affected through the most effective means and advise them of the steps or precautionary measures that they need to take as well as whether the bank would reimburse any losses incurred by them and if so, how they can apply for compensation e.g. by calling enquiry hotlines. Where necessary, the AI

=== PDF page 2 ===
should also notify other affected AIs (so that they can in turn notify their affected customers) as soon as practicable.

Public announcement

In addition to notifying the customers individually, it is also important for the AI concerned to consider making a public announcement where the situation so warrants, such as in the following circumstances:

(a) where the nature of the incident is serious, for example if the incident entails the disruption of any essential and critical banking service channel (e.g. branch services, e-banking, ATM services, etc.) or the disruption may last for a prolonged period of time; or

(b) where a large number of customers have been or may be affected, especially when public announcement is one of the faster or more effective means to alert such customers of the incident than individual notifications.

In notifying the customers and making a public announcement, the AI concerned should include the key facts of the incident and the steps that affected customers need to take in the circumstances in order to gain or regain access to the relevant banking services or to protect their interests.

The above are only the broad principles that an AI should consider and there could be other relevant factors that the AI should also take into account. For example, the need to keep the public informed may need to be weighed against the relevant legal considerations, including where appropriate whether a public announcement may prejudice any ongoing criminal proceedings or any investigation. The important point is that the actions taken to keep the customers and, where appropriate, the public informed of a significant incident should form an integral part of the incident response and management capability of AIs. If in doubt, AIs should consult the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA).

Reporting incident to the HKMA

In addition, once an AI has become aware that a significant incident has occurred, the AI concerned should notify the HKMA immediately and provide it with whatever information is available at the time. For the avoidance of doubt, an AI should not wait until it has rectified the problem before reporting the incident to the HKMA. The HKMA may require the AI concerned to provide further information or updates. Depending on the nature and seriousness of the incident and on whether the incident has wider implications for the general public, the HKMA may make a separate public announcement as appropriate.

=== PDF page 3 ===
Handling of customers’ and media’s enquiry

When handling a significant incident affecting a substantial number of customers, the AI concerned is likely to receive a large number of customer and media enquiries. It is therefore essential for the AI concerned to deploy swiftly adequate resources and communication channels (e.g. customer service hotlines and extended office hours of branch services) to handle such enquiries. In addition, a proper communication strategy should be formulated by the senior management to ensure that consistent and up-to-date messages are conveyed to all relevant parties on a timely basis. The HKMA should be kept informed during the process and copies of public communication materials should be submitted to the HKMA for reference.

AIs should ensure that their staff members are at all times alert to the importance of detecting significant incidents and reporting such incidents to senior management. AIs are expected to ensure that they have in place the appropriate incident response and management capability. The HKMA will continue to assess the adequacy and effectiveness of AIs’ incident response and management capability and procedures through its ongoing supervisory efforts.

  - If it is affected, I hold it, image it later, and say so. LC then uses the Compliance standby device, if logged as working and enrolled, or another permitted route.

   - The transfer/payroll restoration time is unknown.
   - Failover is unverified and on hold.
   - New transfer submissions should be refused or queued visibly, not accepted silently.
3. **For the DPO/LC:** there is no evidence yet of data access or exfiltration. This is unverified. Exfiltration analysis is running, and any indicator will be escalated at once.
4. **For Payments:** the snapshot of in-flight and queued instructions has been preserved. Items in flight stay "status unknown" until independent records show their status.

   - If nothing is spreading, volatile capture (Q01b) runs inside the same 10-minute cap.
2. **By about 08:10: isolate at the network layer.**
   - **Who executes:** Network/firewall operations, on my instruction, under an emergency change record.
   - **What changes:**
     - The payment-gateway segment is put into quarantine: block all inbound and outbound traffic except a single forensic/management VLAN reachable only from the incident response jump host.
     - The route the attacker used is blocked: the admin, jump, remote-access or vendor path into that segment. Which path it was is unverified. Until it is identified, I suspend all privileged and vendor remote sessions into the gateway segment through the privileged access system.
     - Gateway service and admin accounts known to be used in the unauthorised commands are disabled and their sessions and tokens revoked, after a session/token state capture of no more than 10 minutes.
   - **What does not change:** hosts are not powered off, rebooted, restored or failed over. Encrypted hosts stay powered on in quarantine.
3. **Services kept running:**
   - Mobile balance view, branch systems, the core ledger, card authorisation and the channels leading into the gateway stay up.
   - At the boundary of those systems, I block only the specific flows to and from the quarantined gateway segment. Flows that are needed and inspected stay open.
   - The incoming customer channel will fail because the gateway is down. The front end should reject or queue new submissions with a service message, not let them silently sit "in flight". That needs Payments Operations and COM coordination.
4. **Stop and widen triggers:**
   - Widen isolation to a working service only if I find active spread to it, such as encryption, attacker commands or lateral logons. If that would remove a working customer service, I first consult the Head of IT Operations and the CMT chair and log it.
   - Precondition before quarantine is applied: IT Operations confirms the console or out-of-band management route, so we do not lock ourselves out.
   - Validation after quarantine: run reachability tests from both sides of the boundary, and check that mobile balance view and branch systems are healthy. Log the results and the time.
5. **Failover is on hold.** No failover or standby activation until:
   - Failover is shown not to share hosts, accounts, keys or a network path with the affected systems, and
   - The evidence hold for the gateway is released.
   This hold is a security condition. The default if it is not cleared is to hold or use an approved alternate process. The default is never to go ahead. Alternate payment processing needs my written clearance before the CMT chair can activate it.
   Condition per PH01 2.3: I verify it; the latest time is 12:00 HKT, which is 50% of the 24h tolerance; the default is hold; I log a close-out when verified.

Owner: SEC decides. Network/firewall operations and IT Operations execute. I must consult the Head of IT Operations. I must also consult the CMT chair only if a working customer service would be removed.

Timing:
- Spread triage ends 08:10.
- Isolation is in place as soon as possible, target 08:10–08:15.
- First SEC status report to the CMT chair at 09:00, then hourly until containment is confirmed.
- The transfer/payroll tolerance (24h, PH01 4.2) runs out at 08:00 on 17 Nov. 50% is reached at 20:00 on 16 Nov, when the chair tells the Board chair.

Recipient and channel:
- Firewall/network change through the emergency change record.
- Decision log entry (PH01 Annex A fields).
- Verbal briefing to the CMT chair and Head of IT Operations in the CMT room.

Basis:
- **External:**
  - R05, HKMA circular "Incident response and management procedures", 22 Jun 2010, PDF p.1, heading "Immediate incident response". Quote checked against the scan: "The AI concerned should immediately analyse the cause of the incident and as soon as practicable rectify or contain the problem. The top priority should be to safeguard the interests of customers who have been or may be affected by the incident."
    - Authority: HKMA supervisory circular to all AIs.
    - Why it applies: this is a significant incident that disrupts a critical payment service.
    - Left to judgment: how containment is done.
    - Application: contain fast, but keep balance view and branches running because that protects customers.
  - R09, SPM TM-E-1 V.4, PDF p.32, s.8.2.1: "The top priority should be to protect the interests of customers who have been or may be affected by the incident." It applies because mobile/e-banking transfer submission is affected.
  - R02, OCCICS Code of Practice (Generic) v1.0, PDF p.32, s.7.2.3(a)(v)(1). Playbooks must cover "Containing the incident to prevent further harm". This sits under Division 3 obligations (emergency response plan), which apply to a designated CI operator.
    - Authority: Code issued under Cap. 653 s.8. It is not subsidiary legislation, but the Commissioner may issue directions with reference to it (s.1.1.4, PDF p.4).
    - Left to judgment: technical method and sequencing.
- **Internal bank procedure:** PH01 v1.0 (effective 1 Oct 2026).
  - s.7.1 "Isolation order": "SEC isolates at the network layer first: the affected segment and the route used. Hosts are not powered off. Services still working are kept running unless SEC finds active spread to them."
  - s.3, Authority matrix, row "Isolate a system or segment": SEC decides; consult the Head of IT Operations, and the CMT chair if a working customer service will be removed.
  - s.7.3 covers session/token capture of 10 minutes at most before termination.
  - s.8.2 covers SEC's written clearance for alternate processing.
- **Conflict check:** none found. PH01 is consistent with R05, R09 and R02.
- **Professional judgment:** I isolate at the network layer rather than shutting hosts down because that keeps volatile memory and encryption keys that may be in memory. Blocking the gateway at the boundary, rather than shutting down channels, keeps the services that are currently working (balance view, branches) available.

== Q01b: Evidence secured before systems change, and custody ==

Decision and action:
1. **08:00: evidence hold.** I place an evidence hold on the payment gateway hosts and their supporting systems, including directory/admin hosts used in the commands and the jump/PAM path once identified. The hold blocks reboot, rebuild, restore, failover and deletion without my logged release for each item. IT Operations and Payments Operations are told at once.
2. **08:00–08:10: before containment changes anything, capped at 10 minutes, and only if nothing is spreading:**
   - Memory images of one or two representative encrypted gateway hosts.
   - Running processes and network connections.
   - Active sessions and token state for the accounts used.
   - Firewall/PAM session snapshots.
   If anything is spreading, containment goes first and I take these from the isolated hosts afterwards.
3. **After isolation:**
   - Disk images of the affected hosts.
   - Exports of gateway, OS, directory, PAM/session-recording, firewall, EDR and SIEM logs.
   - Copies of the ransom note and encrypted samples. These are handled only inside the evidence process: no outside uploads and no visits to attacker links.
   - Gateway transaction and queue state at failure, for Payments Operations to reconcile in-flight items.
   - Change records.
   - Clock offset readings against the bank's primary time source.
4. **Log retention:** I ask IT Operations to stop log rotation and backup recycling for in-scope systems now. LC issues the written legal hold. The immutable backups are protected: they are not mounted on any affected network.
5. **Suppliers:** I draft written preservation and production requests for any supplier that supports, hosts or has remote access to the gateway by 09:00. LC clears the wording. The vendor relationship owner sends them. Which suppliers are in scope is unknown until the vendor list is checked against the third-party register.
6. **Retained forensic firm:** I engage it at severity 1. Sharing incident data with it is decided jointly by LC and SEC.

Custody:
- **Custodian:** an SEC designate who does not administer the gateway.
- **Fields recorded for each item (PH01 Annex B):**
  - evidence ID, description and source system;
  - HKT acquisition time and clock offset;
  - collector, witness, and tool with version;
  - SHA-256 hash and storage location (offline, encrypted, access-controlled);
  - every transfer (from, to, time, purpose, signatures) and every access.
- **Analysis:** only on verified hash copies.
- **Scope rule:** production artefacts stay held. Analysis copies are offline only. Nothing goes back to production.

Dependency (time-critical): the secure filing terminal is unavailable.
- By 08:30 HKT I will log whether it is within the affected estate or under evidence hold, and whether it can be released.
  - If it is not affected, I release it to LC.
  - If it is affected, I hold it, image it later, and say so. LC then uses the Compliance standby device, if logged as working and enrolled, or another permitted route.
- By 08:30 I will also log whether corporate email is safe. Until then I treat it as not safe.
- Neither check delays any external report. LC's verified telephone route is unaffected.

Owner: SEC. The evidence custodian and SEC forensic analysts execute, with the retained forensic firm assisting. LC owns the legal hold and clearance of supplier requests.

Timing:
- Hold at 08:00.
- Volatile capture by 08:10, capped.
- Filing terminal and email logs by 08:30.
- Supplier preservation requests drafted by 09:00, escalated if not confirmed within 4 hours.
- First evidence register summary in the 09:00 status report.

Recipient and channel:
- Evidence register.
- Decision log.
- Emergency change record.
- Supplier requests sent in writing to the contract contact, with call-back confirmation. Records are received only through bank-hosted encrypted transfer or bank-issued encrypted media, never by email.

Basis:
- **External:**
  - R02, s.7.2.3(a)(v)(2), PDF p.32. Playbooks must cover "Digital evidence handling, including identification, collection, acquisition, preservation of evidence and chain of custody".
  - R02, s.7.2.3(f), PDF p.33: "When balancing the need for timely system recovery and digital evidence handling, the CI operator should prioritize incidents which had impacted business operations, require swift damage containment or need immediate system recovery. Otherwise, more time should be allocated to evidence collection."
    - Application: business operations are affected, so the time spent on evidence before containment is kept short. How long is left to judgment; PH01 sets 10 minutes.
  - R02, s.7.2.3(h), PDF p.33: engage "capable incident response and forensic examination personnel".
  - R03, HKMA Sectoral Code for Designated AIs, PDF p.18, s.6.2.23(c): logs "should be retained for a minimum period of 6 months. Such logs should be secured so that they cannot be deleted or altered". This applies because the gateway is a designated critical computer system (CCS). Missing fact: whether current retention and immutability meet this. To be confirmed.
  - R01, Cap. 653, s.36(2)(b), PDF p.52. The Commissioner may by written notice require the operator "to preserve the state of the system". This is context only and not triggered at C01. Keeping held systems in their current state makes it easy to comply with any such notice.
- **Internal bank procedure:** PH01 v1.0.
  - s.6.1 "Evidence hold": "No reboot, rebuild, restore, failover or deletion on a held system without SEC's logged release for that item."
  - s.6.2: "Collection of volatile evidence before containment is capped at 10 minutes."
  - s.6.3 "Custody": "The evidence custodian is an SEC designate who does not administer the affected systems."
  - Also: s.6.4 (clocks), s.6.6 (attacker material), s.6.7 (supplier preservation requests within one hour), s.5.6 and 5.7 (30-minute terminal and email logs), s.17.1 (LC legal hold), Annex B.
- **Conflict check:** none found. PH01 s.6.2 matches R02 s.7.2.3(f).

== Facts I pass to the incident team (CMT/LC/COM) at the 08:15 briefing and 09:00 report ==
1. **For LC:**
   - Confirmed and unverified items for the HKMA and Cap. 653 reports: gateway encrypted by unauthorised commands; core function (domestic transfers and payroll) disrupted from about 08:00 or earlier. The exact detection time comes from the SIEM timeline.
   - Containment checkbox status for the Cap. 653 forms (R02 Annex, PDF p.45: segments isolated, accounts removed, IPs blocked).
   - Filing terminal and email status by 08:30.
2. **For COM and Payments:**
   - Balance view and branches are working and are being kept running.
   - The transfer/payroll restoration time is unknown.
   - Failover is unverified and on hold.
   - New transfer submissions should be refused or queued visibly, not accepted silently.
3. **For the DPO/LC:** there is no evidence yet of data access or exfiltration. This is unverified. Exfiltration analysis is running, and any indicator will be escalated at once.
4. **For Payments:** the snapshot of in-flight and queued instructions has been preserved. Items in flight stay "status unknown" until independent records show their status.
5. **Open dependencies:**
   - Attacker entry route and credential (drives vendor lockout).
   - Supplier list for preservation requests.
   - Clean status of failover and the immutable backup.
   - 12:00 security-clearance checkpoint for alternate processing.

[PH01] Lan Tidal Bank Cyber Incident Response Playbook (1.0, effective 1 October 2026; internal bank procedure)

[Internal bank procedure. This document has no PDF. Each "PDF page" below holds one part of the playbook: page 1 is the title block and section 1, pages 2 to 18 are sections 2 to 18, and page 19 is Annexes A and B. Cite it by version and section number.]

=== PDF page 10 ===
## 10. Customer notification

10.1 **Who.** COM drafts and sends; the CMT chair approves the audience; LC clears the text; SEC and Operations confirm each factual line.

10.2 **Approved channels.** Personal call from a named team with an offer to call back on the number on the customer's card; notice in the authenticated secure inbox; letter. SMS, push and email may carry an alert but never a link. The secure inbox is used only after SEC logs that it is trusted; by default (2.3), written notices go by letter.

10.3 **Delivery register.** From the first notice, COM keeps a register with one row per customer: batch, data types, contact details used, each attempt with time, channel and outcome, and proof of delivery. Approval and scheduling are not delivery. Completion figures go to LC daily.

10.4 **Widening the notification scope.**
(a) Customers whose exposure is confirmed, and customers for whom there is evidence that their data was accessed, copied or misused, are notified as soon as practicable. They are not held back for the wider review.
(b) No later than 12 hours after the first confirmation of exposure, the DPO and LC review, with SEC's evidence, whether the scope should be widened. The CMT chair decides and logs the decision and the reasons.
(c) For a larger group whose exposure is possible but not shown, the scope is set by evidence and risk: evidence that their records were accessed or copied; publication or offer of the data; reports of misuse; the sensitivity of the data types; and whether their records were held in the same place as confirmed records. An unverified claim, or the size of the data store, does not by itself make everyone in the store a notification batch.
(d) Where part of the group is not notified yet, the reason is logged, and the decision is reviewed whenever new evidence arrives and at least every 24 hours until the scope is settled. The CMT chair decides whether a public statement under section 11 covers customers not notified individually.

10.5 **Changed contact details.** Contact details are taken only from the bank's verified records. Details changed after the incident started are checked by the Fraud team before use.

10.6 **Duplicates.** A customer with evidenced delivery of current content gets nothing further until there is something new. A customer with no evidenced delivery gets one consolidated notice.

=== PDF page 11 ===
## 11. Public statements and media

11.1 The CMT chair is the only spokesperson. Staff refer all media enquiries to COM.

11.2 **Cadence.** While a critical operation is disrupted, COM publishes a dated status update at least every six hours between 07:00 and 22:00, and at once on any change in service status. Each update states what is confirmed, what is being verified, what customers can do and when the next update is due.

11.3 **Fixed lines.** The bank never denies receipt of a demand. It states whether a payment has been made only as a verified present fact. It does not name the attacker, the vendor, the affected system or the bank's designation status.

11.4 **Figures.** A figure is published only if its owner has confirmed it from a record. Otherwise the update says the figure is being checked and when it will be given.

11.5 **Closing update.** A closing update is issued only when: the service runs in production and SEC confirms it is stable; queued instructions are settled or returned; the notification register shows evidenced delivery to all affected customers; every open case has a named owner; and LC confirms the regulators have been told. Until then updates continue.

=== PDF page 12 ===
## 12. Ransom and extortion

12.1 **Policy.** The Board's policy is that the bank does not pay a ransom. Any departure is for the Board alone.

12.2 **Legal gates before the Board may consider a departure.** LC confirms in writing: the position under the Organized and Serious Crimes Ordinance (Cap. 455), including any disclosure and consent; screening of the recipient under the United Nations (Anti-Terrorism Measures) Ordinance (Cap. 575); sanctions screening by external counsel; the Police view; and the insurer's position. Treasury holds all preparatory steps (virtual-asset accounts, purchases, intermediaries) until the Board decides.

12.3 **Contact with an attacker.** None, unless the CMT chair authorises it in writing on a joint LC and SEC recommendation, for a stated limited purpose, after consulting the Police. Contact is made only by one designated specialist on a segregated channel, with a full transcript. Staff, branches, COM and vendors never reply to an attacker; they pass any message to SEC.

12.4 **Insurer.** The CFO notifies the cyber insurer within 24 hours of declaration.

[PH01] Lan Tidal Bank Cyber Incident Response Playbook (1.0, effective 1 October 2026; internal bank procedure)

[Internal bank procedure. This document has no PDF. Each "PDF page" below holds one part of the playbook: page 1 is the title block and section 1, pages 2 to 18 are sections 2 to 18, and page 19 is Annexes A and B. Cite it by version and section number.]

=== PDF page 16 ===
## 16. Third parties holding incident data

16.1 Data goes to a forensic firm or other third party only under a signed agreement that limits use to the incident and to the bank's instructions, requires confidentiality, keeps processing in Hong Kong, forbids sub-contracting and onward disclosure without consent, requires immediate reporting of any loss, gives the bank audit rights, and requires return or destruction with a certificate.

16.2 By default the firm receives a minimised data set with customer personal data masked. Full images are examined only inside the bank's laboratory. A full copy leaves the bank only with LC's and SEC's written approval.

[R11] PCPD Guidance on Data Breach Handling and Data Breach Notifications (June 2023)

[Text layer of the PDF with the same name, one block per PDF page. The PDF is the authoritative copy.]

=== PDF page 3 ===
PREPARING FOR CONTINGENCY – DATA BREACH RESPONSE PLAN
A data breach response plan is a document setting
out how an organisation will respond in the event
of a data breach. A comprehensive data breach
response plan helps ensure a quick response to and
effective management of a data breach. The plan
should outline a set of procedures to be followed
in the event of a data breach and the data user’s
strategy for identifying, containing, assessing and
managing the impact brought about by the incident
from start to finish. A prompt response to a data
breach may substantially minimise and contain the
impact of a breach.
The plan is recommended to cover the
following aspects (non-exhaustive):
ØØ A description of what constitutes a data
breach with examples tailored to the
nature of the organisation, and the criteria
that trigger the implementation of the data
breach response plan
ØØ An internal incident notification
procedure to escalate the breach to the
senior management, the data protection
officer and/or dedicated data breach
response team, incorporating a standard
form to facilitate the reporting of the
required information
ØØ The designation of the roles and
responsibilities of members of the
dedicated breach response team (e.g., the
data protection officer may assume overall
responsibility for handling a data breach
incident; the information technology
department for identifying the location of
potentially compromised data and taking
remedial measures; and the customer
service department for addressing the
issues of affected individuals and for
providing updates to customers)
ØØ ØØ A contact list with contact details of all
breach response team members (e.g., the
core management, chief data protection
officer, information technology experts,
risk management and human resources
professionals)
A risk assessment workflow to assess the
likelihood and severity of the harm caused
to the affected data subjects as a result of
the breach
ØØ A containment strategy for containing
and remedying the breach
ØØ A communication plan covering the
criteria and threshold for determining
whether the affected data subjects,
regulatory authorities and other
relevant parties should be notified;
the kind of information that must be
provided; the point of contact in the
organisation responsible for liaising with
the stakeholders; and the methods of
notification
ØØ An investigation procedure f o r
investigating the breach and reporting the
results to the senior management
ØØ A record-keeping policy to ensure that
the incident is properly documented as
the relevant records may be required by
regulatory authorities or law enforcement
agencies
ØØ A post-incident review mechanism for
identifying areas that require improvement
to prevent future recurrence
ØØ A training or drill plan to ensure that all
relevant staff can follow the procedures
properly when dealing with a data breach
Guidance on Data Breach Handling and Data Breach Notifications 3
June 2023

=== PDF page 4 ===
HANDLING DATA BREACHES
The proper handling and management of a data
breach demonstrates the data user’s commitment to
tackling the problem and may substantially reduce
the impact of a breach on affected individuals
and the potential reputational damage to the
organisation. The following steps are recommended
when handling a data breach.
Step 1: Immediate gathering of essential information
As a starting point, the data user shall promptly
gather all relevant information of the data
breach to assess the impact on data subjects and
to identify appropriate mitigation measures.
Questions such as the following should be
addressed:
•
When did the breach occur?
•
Where did the breach occur?
•
How was the breach detected and by whom?
•
What was the cause of the breach?
•
What kind of personal data was involved?
•
How many data subjects might be affected?
•
What harm may have been caused to those
affected individuals?
The staff members who first discover the breach
should consider whether to escalate the incident
to the dedicated data breach response team/senior
management/data protection officer, according
to the procedures laid down in the data breach
response plan.
Step 2: Containing the data breach
After detecting the breach and conducting
an initial assessment, the data user should
immediately take steps to contain the breach as
effectively as possible. Remedial actions to lessen
the harm or damage that may be caused to the
affected data subjects should be taken.
Depending on the categories of personal
data involved and the severity of the breach,
the following containment measures (non-
exhaustive) may be considered:
ØØ ØØ ØØ ØØ Conducting a thorough search for the lost
items containing personal data
Requesting the unintended recipients of
emails/letters/fax to delete or return the
mistakenly sent documents
Requesting internet companies to remove
any relevant cached links from their search
engines
Shutting down or isolating the compromised/
breached system/server and thoroughly
checking whether other interconnected
systems containing personal data are
affected
ØØ Disabling system functions that may be
relevant to the breach
ØØ Fixing any bugs or errors that may have
caused the breach
ØØ ØØ Alerting banks or credit card companies,
which may help reduce the risk of financial
losses for the affected data subjects
Keeping records of the occurrence of the
breach and all follow-up actions taken to
facilitate investigations and for the taking
of corrective actions
ØØ Notifying the relevant law enforcement
agencies if identity theft or other criminal
activities have been or are likely to be
committed
ØØ Requiring the data processor to take
immediate remedial measures and to
notify the data user of the progress in the
event that the data breach is caused by an
act or omission by the data processor
ØØ Remotely wiping a lost or stolen electronic
device
Guidance on Data Breach Handling and Data Breach Notifications 4
June 2023

=== PDF page 5 ===
ØØ Changing users' passwords and system
configurations to block any (further)
unauthorised access
ØØ Removing the access rights of users
suspected to have committed or
contributed to the data breach
ØØ Keeping a proper record of the compromised
system for further investigation
ØØ Considering whether technical assistance
is required
Step 3: Assessing the risk of harm
Once all essential information has been gathered,
the data users should then ensure that they
understand the risks of harm that may be caused to
the affected individuals, so that they can take steps
to limit the impact. The possible harm caused by a
data breach may include:
•
Threats to personal safety
•
Identity theft
•
Financial loss
•
Humiliation or loss of dignity, damage to
reputation or relationships
•
Loss of business or employment opportunities
The extent of the harm suffered by the
affected data subjects in a data breach
depends on:
ØØ The kind and sensitivity of the personal
data being leaked: generally, the more
sensitive the data, the higher the risk of
harm that may be caused to the affected
data subjects
ØØ The amount of personal data involved:
in general, the greater the volume of
personal data leaked, the more serious the
consequences will be
ØØ The circumstances of the data breach:
online data leakage is difficult to be
effectively contained and the further
dissemination and use of the leaked data
is thus a risk. However, if the recipients of
the data are known and traceable, the data
breach may be easier to contain
ØØ The nature of harm
ØØ The likelihood of identity theft or fraud:
sometimes, the leaked data, either
independently in itself or when combined
with other data, can facilitate the
commission of identity theft or fraud. For
example, a combination of Hong Kong
Identity Card information, date of birth,
address, credit card details and bank
account information is more likely to result
in identity theft
ØØ Whether a backup of the lost data is
available
ØØ Whether the leaked data are adequately
encrypted, anonymised or otherwise
rendered inaccessible, e.g., if access is
password-protected
ØØ ØØ The duration of the breach
Whether the breach is an isolated incident
or a systematic problem
ØØ In the case of physical loss, whether the
lost items have been found before they
could be accessed or copied
ØØ Whether effective mitigation/remedial
measures have been taken after the breach
has occurred
ØØ The ability of the data subjects to avoid or
mitigate possible harm
ØØ The affected data subjects’ reasonable
expectations of personal data privacy
Guidance on Data Breach Handling and Data Breach Notifications 5
June 2023
